kurals.tamil:
மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர் அவரன்ன
ஒப்பாரி யாங்கண்ட தில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Makkale polvar kayavar avaranna
oppaari yaangkanda thil.
kurals.meaning: The base look exactly like human beings; I have never seen a likeness as perfect as theirs between any two other kinds of things.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a shiny plastic apple in a fruit bowl. It looks just like a real apple, but you cannot eat it. Some people are like that: they look like everyone else on the outside, but inside they lack the kindness and goodness that make a real person.
kurals.university: Kayamai (கயமை, 'baseness') closes the Porutpal and its Kudiyiyal section, as a dark mirror to the preceding chapters on nobility of birth, honour, greatness, perfect goodness and courtesy (chs. 96-100). The first couplet is a famous piece of irony: kayavar (கயவர், 'the base') are makkale polvar (மக்களே போல்வர், 'just like humans'), and oppaari (ஒப்பாரி, 'resemblance') so exact is found nowhere else. Parimelazhagar and the commentators who follow him (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan) read it as saying the base share only the outward form of humanity, so that the likeness is complete in shape and absent in substance; Solomon Pappaiah adds that no animal or bird species shows such a perfect double. Pope renders it 'The base resemble men in outward form, I ween; / But counterpart exact to them I've never seen.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arrogance, pride, anger, conceit, harshness and ignorance—these qualities belong to those of demonic nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names the traits that mark the asuric (demonic) nature in people who are outwardly human.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita locates what is base not in a person's form but in qualities that hollow out their humanity.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a strong thematic fit on inner baseness, though the Gita lacks the Kural's irony about outward resemblance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus compares hypocrites to painted tombs that look fine outside and are full of decay inside.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's base person is likewise perfect on the outside and empty within.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); close on the contrast between outward appearance and inner reality.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes people who have every human faculty but do not use them, and so fall below the animals.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says such people have the human frame but not what makes it human.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; near one-to-one on human form without human substance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that being truly human is a moral achievement, especially where others fail at it.
judaism.tie_back: Hillel's saying assumes the Kural's point, that many who look like men are not men in the full sense.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:5 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong fit on 'man' as a moral rather than physical category, though it exhorts rather than describes the base.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by mere eloquence nor by beauty of form does a man become accomplished, if he is jealous, selfish and deceitful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says outward gifts like fine speech or good looks count for nothing in a person who is envious, selfish and deceitful.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, outward appearance cannot make up for a base character.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; close on form versus character.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The base in prosperity will not do these things which those who are of high birth will do even in adversity. Though one place rings (of gold) upon the tusks of a hog, O thou who hast eyes like a lance! it will never become a warlike elephant.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar says that dressing up a hog's tusks in gold rings does not turn it into a war elephant, and outward finery does not change the nature of the base.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the stanza says the base may look like the real thing but stay what they are underneath.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 36.8, chapter 'Baseness or Envy' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text with its own chapter on baseness, a strong fit on appearance versus nature.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Diogenes the Cynic is said to have lit a lamp in broad daylight and walked about saying he was looking for a man.
greek_mythology.explanation: The joke was that the streets were full of people but he could not find a real human being among them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Diogenes makes the Kural's ironic point: many look like men, but few are.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Well-attested anecdote, given here as a paraphrase; it is Greek philosophical lore rather than myth, but very close to the Kural's irony.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle writes that man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but when separated from law and justice he is the worst of all.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, being human is fulfilled only through virtue and justice; without them a human being sinks below the beasts.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, separates the human form from the human excellence that should fill it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of a well-known passage, not verified verbatim this session; a strong thematic fit.

kurals.tamil:
நன்றறி வாரிற் கயவர் திருவுடையர்
நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nandrari vaarir kayavar thiruvudaiyar
nenjaththu avalam ilar.
kurals.meaning: The base are luckier than those who know what is good, because no worry ever troubles their hearts.
kurals.elementary: Think of two children who broke a vase. One feels bad, says sorry, and worries about it all day. The other just shrugs and goes on playing. The second one looks happier, but only because he does not care about doing right. The Kural is joking: being carefree like that is nothing to envy.
kurals.university: The couplet is sarcastic praise. Nandru arivaar (நன்றறிவார், 'those who know the good') are contrasted with kayavar, who are thiru udaiyar (திருவுடையர், 'possessed of fortune, blessed'), because they have no avalam (அவலம், 'anxiety, grief') in the nenjam (heart). Parimelazhagar explains that the wise are anxious about what is right and its consequences in this world and the next, while the base feel no such care; Puliyur Kesikan glosses nandru as 'what is truly beneficial to oneself'. Kalaignar keeps the irony explicit ('in one way they are fortunate'). Pope: 'Than those of grateful heart the base must luckier be, / Their minds from every anxious thought are free!' Pope's 'grateful' reflects a reading of nandri as 'gratitude'; most Tamil commentators take nandru as 'the good'. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And that happiness which is blind to self-realization, which is delusion from beginning to end and which arises from sleep, laziness and illusion is said to be of the nature of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita names a kind of happiness that comes from dullness and delusion and calls it tamasic, the lowest of the three kinds.
hinduism.tie_back: The carefree ease the Kural mocks in the base is just this blind, tamasic happiness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.39 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a strong fit on the low quality of the base man's contentment, though the Gita does not use irony.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued like other men.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist admits he envied the wicked because they seemed free of the troubles that weigh on good people.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's ironic observation that the base seem luckier because nothing troubles them.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); near one-to-one, and the psalm, like the Kural, goes on to show this ease is no real blessing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Let them eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by [false] hope, for they are going to know.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an lets the heedless enjoy their carefree life for now, warning that they will learn the truth later.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows the base enjoying an untroubled life that is not really fortunate.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; strong fit on carefree heedlessness, with a warning the Kural leaves implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “it is not in our hands [to explain the reason] either of the security of the wicked, or even of the afflictions of the righteous.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yannai admits that we cannot explain why the wicked live at ease while the righteous suffer.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah faces the same puzzle the Kural turns into sarcasm: the base seem secure while the good are troubled.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:15 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; close on the ease of the wicked, though Avot speaks of outward security rather than an untroubled heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easy is life for the shameless one who is impudent as a crow, is backbiting and forward, arrogant and corrupt.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that life is easy for the shameless, while the next verse says it is hard for the modest who seek purity.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's ironic claim that the base, free of conscience, have the easier life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; near one-to-one, especially read with verse 245 on the hard life of the conscientious.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man attached to pleasures and amusements will be caught in the trap (of deceit). (He thinks): 'I never saw the next world, but I have seen with my own eyes the pleasures of this life.'”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira describes the fool who lives carelessly for present pleasure, untroubled by thoughts of karma or the next life, and the lecture goes on to show his dread at death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is free of worry for the same reason: he does not care about what is good or what follows from his deeds.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong canonical fit on the careless ease of the ignorant, though without the Kural's sarcasm.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato's Gorgias, Polus argues that the unjust tyrant Archelaus, who seized power by murder, is happy, and Socrates insists that the wicked man is the most miserable of all.
greek_mythology.explanation: Polus judges by appearances: the wrongdoer seems to prosper without care, while Socrates holds that injustice ruins the soul.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's sarcasm makes Socrates' point: the base only seem fortunate.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known exchange, not quoted; Greek philosophical dialogue rather than myth, a reasonable but partial fit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.”
philosophy.explanation: Mill argues that the restless discontent of a thoughtful person is worth more than the easy contentment of someone who does not know what he is missing.
philosophy.tie_back: Mill states plainly what the Kural says through irony: the untroubled base are not the truly fortunate.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the Project Gutenberg text; near one-to-one on the thoughtless person's contentment.

kurals.tamil:
தேவர் அனையர் கயவர் அவருந்தாம்
மேவன செய்தொழுக லான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thevar anaiyar kayavar avarundhaam
mevana seydhozhuga laan.
kurals.meaning: The base are like the gods, because they too do whatever they please.
kurals.elementary: Gods in stories can do anything they like, and nobody can tell them off. A spoiled bully acts the same way, doing whatever he wants without thinking of anyone else. The Kural jokes that this makes him 'like a god', but it really means he has no self-control at all.
kurals.university: Another ironic comparison: kayavar are thevar anaiyar (தேவர் அனையர், 'like the gods') because they too live mevana seydhu (மேவன செய்து, 'doing what they desire'). Puliyur Kesikan spells out the logic: like the gods, they have no one to restrain them (தம்மை நியமிப்பவர் இல்லாமல்), and Solomon Pappaiah glosses it the same way. Parimelazhagar's reading is that the gods are free because they stand above rules, while the base are 'free' because they ignore them, so the likeness is pure mockery. Kalaignar points to the gods 'of the Puranas' who act on every wish. Pope: 'The base are as the Gods; they too / Do ever what they list to do!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But he who discards scriptural injunctions and acts according to his own whims attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme destination.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a person who throws off all guidance and lives by whim reaches no good end.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's base man who 'does as he pleases' is exactly the whim-driven man the Gita condemns.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.23 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; close on acting by whim (kama-karatah), though without the ironic comparison to gods.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.”
christianity.explanation: The serpent tempts Eve with the promise that by grasping what is forbidden she will become like the gods.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural mocks the same delusion: acting without restraint makes one 'like the gods' only in a false and ruinous sense.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); a reasonable fit on false godlikeness through self-will, though the context is temptation rather than character.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you seen he who has taken as his god his [own] desire”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the person who makes his own desires his god and so loses guidance.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's base man treats his wishes as law, as if he were a god; the Qur'an says he has made his wishes his god.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; near one-to-one on desire treated as divine law.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
judaism.explanation: The book of Judges ends by describing a time of chaos when everyone did whatever he wanted.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats doing whatever one pleases, with no restraint, as a sign of moral collapse.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong fit on unrestrained self-will, though it describes a society rather than a type of person.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Formerly this mind wandered about as it liked, where it wished and according to its pleasure, but now I shall thoroughly master it with wisdom as a mahout controls with his ankus an elephant in rut.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts a mind that roams wherever it likes with a mind tamed by wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the untamed mind of this verse, going 'where it wished and according to its pleasure'.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; strong on acting as one pleases, though framed as self-taming rather than criticism of others.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The worthy, though they have attained the wealth of the world, will at no time indulge in haughty speech, but if the mean have acquired the wealth of one cani (1/80 part) added to one muntheri (1/320) they will regard themselves as great as Indra king of heaven.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar mocks the mean man who, with a tiny bit of wealth, thinks himself equal to Indra, king of the gods.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Naladiyar sarcastically likens the base to a god, a comparison that exposes their smallness.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 35.6, chapter 'Meanness' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (italics on cani and muntheri dropped); a Tamil Jain text with the same ironic god-comparison, though its point is vanity rather than lack of restraint.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Salmoneus, a mortal king, set himself up as Zeus, driving a chariot that dragged bronze kettles to imitate thunder and hurling torches as lightning, until Zeus struck him down.
greek_mythology.explanation: Salmoneus believed that doing whatever he liked made him the equal of the king of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Salmoneus is the Kural's base man who is 'like the gods' only in his unrestrained self-will.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, The Library 1.9.7 (tr. J. G. Frazer)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested myth; strong fit on false godlikeness, though Salmoneus is punished for impiety rather than mocked for baseness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Locke distinguishes liberty from licence: the state of nature is a state of liberty, but not one in which a person may do whatever he pleases, because reason and the law of nature still bind him.
philosophy.explanation: For Locke, true freedom is bounded by moral law; doing anything one likes is licence, not liberty.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's base man mistakes licence for the freedom of the gods.
philosophy.source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, ch. 2 §6 (1690)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not verified verbatim this session; a strong conceptual fit.

kurals.tamil:
அகப்பட்டி ஆவாரைக் காணின் அவரின்
மிகப்பட்டுச் செம்மாக்கும் கீழ்.
kurals.transliteration:
Agappatti aavaaraik kaanin avarin
migappattuch chemmaakkum keezh.
kurals.meaning: When the base meet people whose conduct is even lower than their own, they swell with pride at being better than them.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a child who got a bad mark on a test. Instead of trying to do better, he finds someone who did even worse and says, 'Ha, at least I'm better than you!' That is what the Kural means: base people feel big by looking down on someone lower.
kurals.university: Keezh (கீழ், 'the low, the base') is the chapter's second word for its subject. The difficult word agappatti (அகப்பட்டி) has divided commentators: Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesikan take aavaar as those who behave even more basely, so that the base man sees them and becomes migappattu (மிகப்பட்டு, 'superior, exalted') and semmaakkum (செம்மாக்கும், 'struts, exults'); Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as 'those who live like dogs, as they please'; Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as 'those beneath them'. The common sense is that baseness takes its self-esteem from someone lower. Pope's 'When base men those behold of conduct vile, / They straight surpass them, and exulting smile' follows the 'conduct vile' reading. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I am the richest man, surrounded by aristocratic relatives. There is none so powerful and happy as I am.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita gives the inner voice of the demonic person, who measures himself against others and swells with pride.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's base man also struts by comparing himself to others he thinks lower.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.13-15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com (excerpt from a three-verse passage); reasonable fit on comparative pride, though the Gita's boaster compares himself to everyone, not to those beneath him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable, the Pharisee builds himself up by pointing to a man he considers lower than himself.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's base man exactly: he feels superior by looking down on someone else.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); near one-to-one on pride drawn from comparison with someone deemed lower.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people; perhaps they may be better than them”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids mocking others, since those looked down on may be better in God's sight.
islam.tie_back: It forbids exactly the contemptuous comparison that the Kural says is how the base feel superior.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a strong fit on contempt for those thought lower.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is he that is honored? He who honors his fellow human beings”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma teaches that real honour comes from honouring others, not from rising above them.
judaism.tie_back: This is the opposite of the Kural's base man, who seeks honour by despising those beneath him.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a reasonable contrastive fit, though it states the positive ideal rather than describing the base.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whosoever debased by his pride, exalts himself and belittles other — know him as an outcast.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Discourse on Outcasts, the Buddha says one becomes truly low by deeds, including exalting oneself and belittling others.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha's 'outcast' and the Kural's keezh are the same figure: the man who rises in his own eyes by putting others down.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7, v. 17 (tr. Piyadassi Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; near one-to-one, and the sutta, like this chapter, defines baseness by conduct.

jainism.quote_or_event: “the base man is mighty in speaking harsh words. He regards no one, laughs at the misery of others, grows more and more enraged and will continually reproach others.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar describes the base man who respects no one and laughs at others' misfortunes.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's keezh, he gains his sense of superiority from looking down on those worse off.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 35.8, chapter 'Meanness' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text, strong on contempt for others, though it does not specify those lower than himself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theophrastus' sketch of the arrogant man shows someone who looks down on everyone, makes others wait on him and treats those he thinks beneath him with contempt.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greek character sketch catalogues the small habits of a man who builds himself up by belittling others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the same comparative pride as the Kural's base man, though less sharply focused on those even lower.
greek_mythology.source: Theophrastus, Characters, 'The Arrogant Man' (tr. R. C. Jebb)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: General paraphrase, not verified this session; Greek literature rather than myth, and only a next-best match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hobbes defines 'sudden glory' as the passion behind laughter, caused either by something one does oneself or by seeing some defect in another, by comparison with which one suddenly applauds oneself; he adds that it is most common in those who know they have few abilities.
philosophy.explanation: Hobbes explains contemptuous laughter as a way the weak feel strong by noticing the weakness of others.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's psychology exactly: the base exult on finding someone lower than themselves.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of a well-known passage, not verified verbatim this session; near one-to-one in idea.

kurals.tamil:
அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம் எச்சம்
அவாவுண்டேல் உண்டாம் சிறிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Achchame keezhgaladhu aasaaram echcham
avaavundel undaam siridhu.
kurals.meaning: Fear is the main reason the base behave properly; beyond that, they show a little good conduct only when they want something.
kurals.elementary: Some children only behave when the teacher is watching, or when they hope to get a sweet. When nobody is looking and there is no prize, they misbehave. The Kural says base people are like that: they are good only out of fear or for a reward.
kurals.university: Aasaaram (ஆசாரம், from Sanskrit ācāra, 'right conduct, propriety') in the base has two sources only: achcham (அச்சம், 'fear') and, as echcham (எச்சம், 'remainder'), avaa (அவா, 'desire, greed'). Parimelazhagar specifies the fear as fear of the king's punishment, and Puliyur Kesikan follows ('அரசரால் துன்பம் வரும் என்னும் அச்சம்'); Solomon Pappaiah likewise reads it as fear of the government. The second line says that if desire for some gain is present, a little more good conduct appears. The couplet thus defines the base by motive: they have no inner love of virtue. Pope: 'Fear is the base man's virtue; if that fail, / Intense desire some little may avail.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The whole world is kept in order by punishment, for a guiltless man is hard to find; through fear of punishment the whole world yields the enjoyments (which it owes).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that fear of the king's rod (danda) is what keeps most people in line.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim about the base: fear of punishment, not virtue, produces their good behaviour.
hinduism.source: Laws of Manu 7.22 (tr. G. Bühler, SBE 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; close on fear of royal punishment, though Manu applies it to the whole world, not only the base.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:”
christianity.explanation: Paul says the authorities are something to fear only for wrongdoers, and that doing good earns praise.
christianity.tie_back: The verse names the two motives the Kural assigns to the base, fear of rulers and hope of reward.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); a strong fit on fear and reward as motives, though Paul is not describing the base specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “You [believers] are more fearful within their breasts than Allāh. That is because they are a people who do not understand.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says the hypocrites fear people more than God, so their conduct is governed by fear of others, not by faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's base, their behaviour comes from fear of an outside power rather than inner conviction.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a reasonable fit on fear as the governing motive, though the context is wartime hypocrisy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina teaches that fear of the ruling power is what keeps people from devouring one another.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line: fear of authority is what keeps the base in order.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:2 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; near one-to-one on fear of government as the restraint on wrongdoing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who appropriates be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he appropriates his friend's wealth, (ii) he gives little and asks much, (iii) he does his duty out of fear, (iv) he associates for his own advantage.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a false friend who does what he should only out of fear and for his own gain.
buddhism.tie_back: These are exactly the two motives the Kural gives the base: fear first, and a little more good conduct when there is something to gain.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (tr. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; close on fear and self-interest as motives, though framed as a false friend rather than the base in general.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Better it is that I should subdue my Self by self-control and penance, than be subdued by others with fetters and corporal punishment.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching sets self-restraint chosen from within against restraint forced from outside by chains and punishment.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the one who must be 'subdued by others' through fear, because he will not restrain himself.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong canonical contrast between inner restraint and restraint by fear of punishment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato's Republic, Glaucon tells the story of Gyges, a shepherd who found a ring that made him invisible and then used it to seduce the queen, kill the king and seize the throne, arguing that anyone would act unjustly if he could do so without fear of being caught.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story suggests that for many people, justice is only fear of consequences.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Glaucon's Gyges is the Kural's base man: remove the fear and his good conduct disappears.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; near one-to-one on goodness that exists only through fear.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For these do not by nature obey the sense of shame, but only fear, and do not abstain from bad acts because of their baseness but through fear of punishment”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that most people are kept from wrongdoing not by shame or love of the noble but by fear of punishment, which is why laws are needed.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle states the Kural's point almost word for word, even naming 'baseness'.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.9 (1179b) (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; near one-to-one on fear as the only restraint of the base.

kurals.tamil:
அறைபறை அன்னர் கயவர்தாம் கேட்ட
மறைபிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்க லான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Araiparai annar kayavardhaam ketta
maraipirarkku uyththuraikka laan.
kurals.meaning: The base are like a drum that is beaten to announce news, because they carry every secret they hear straight to others.
kurals.elementary: Long ago, a town crier would beat a big drum and shout the news to the whole village. Some people are like that drum: tell them a secret, and they run off and tell everyone. A good friend keeps a secret safe.
kurals.university: The simile is the araiparai (அறைபறை), the drum beaten in the streets to proclaim royal announcements; Kalaignar names it the thamukku. The base hear a marai (மறை, 'secret, confidential matter') and uyththu uraikkum (உய்த்துரைக்கும், 'carry it to others and tell it'), going out of their way to spread it, as Mu. Varadarasanar stresses (வலிய கொண்டுபோய்). Parimelazhagar's point is that the drum and the base both broadcast what they receive, with no judgement about whether it should be told. Sivayogi Sivakumar adds that the base repeat what they do not themselves understand. Pope: 'The base are like the beaten drum; for, when they hear / The sound the secret out in every neighbour's ear.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king whose secret plans other people, (though) assembled (for the purpose), do not discover, (will) enjoy the whole earth, though he be poor in treasure.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu stresses that secret counsel must be guarded, and the following verses warn the king to keep it from those likely to betray it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the kind of person Manu warns against: one who cannot be trusted with a secret.
hinduism.source: Laws of Manu 7.148 (tr. G. Bühler, SBE 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; only a next-best match, since it praises secrecy in statecraft rather than condemning a gossip, and Manu's list of likely betrayers (7.149-150) reflects the prejudices of its era.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the gossip who spreads secrets with the trustworthy person who keeps them.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's drum-like base man set beside the faithful friend.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); near one-to-one on revealing secrets.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when there comes to them something [i.e., information] about [public] security or fear, they spread it around.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes people who broadcast sensitive news instead of taking it to those who can judge it.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's base, they pass on whatever they hear without restraint.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; strong on spreading information, though the context is public and military news rather than private confidences.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not deal basely with members of your people.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah's command, which the translators note refers to slander and is often rendered 'do not go about as a talebearer', forbids spreading harmful talk.
judaism.tie_back: The Torah calls talebearing 'dealing basely', the very vice the Kural assigns to the base.
judaism.source: Leviticus 19:16 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria with its footnote on the idiom; strong on talebearing, though it concerns slander generally rather than secrets specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he reveals his secrets, (ii) he conceals one's own secrets, (iii) in misfortune he does not forsake one”
buddhism.explanation: Among the marks of a true friend, the Buddha lists keeping one's friend's secrets hidden.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the opposite: whatever is told to him in confidence he broadcasts.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (tr. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a reasonable contrastive fit, stating the virtue rather than condemning the vice.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists five transgressions of the layperson's vow of truthfulness, including rahobhyakhyana (divulging what was said or done in private) and sakaramantrabheda (revealing another's confidential intentions).
jainism.explanation: In Jain ethics, spreading secrets is not just bad manners but a breach of the vow of truth (satya-anuvrata).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's base man commits exactly these faults by carrying every secret to others.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.26 (numbering of the Digambara recension; via wisdomlib.org glossary of satyanuvrata)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the sutra's list, confirmed on wisdomlib.org; a canonical text and a close fit on divulging secrets.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas's barber, who alone knew the king had ass's ears, could not bear to keep the secret, so he dug a hole and whispered it into the ground; reeds grew there and whispered the secret to everyone when the wind blew.
greek_mythology.explanation: The barber's need to tell what he knew ended with the secret broadcast to the whole world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The barber, and the reeds that spread his whisper, are like the Kural's drum that carries what it hears to everyone.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth (Roman telling of a Greek tale); close on a secret that cannot be kept.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch's essay On Talkativeness describes the chatterer who cannot hold anything he hears, comparing his speech to leaking vessels and his secrets to things that slip out at once, and praises silence as the mark of a trustworthy person.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats the inability to keep a confidence as a serious defect of character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's base man is Plutarch's chatterer, who passes on every secret he hears.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia: De garrulitate (On Talkativeness) (tr. W. C. Helmbold)
philosophy._accuracy_note: General paraphrase of the essay's theme, not verified verbatim this session; a strong thematic fit.

kurals.tamil:
ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார் கயவர் கொடிறுடைக்கும்
கூன்கையர் அல்லா தவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Eerngai vidhiraar kayavar kodirudaikkum
koonkaiyar allaa thavarkku.
kurals.meaning: The base will not even shake the crumbs off their wet hand after eating for anyone except those who would smash their jaw with a clenched fist.
kurals.elementary: After lunch, a few crumbs stick to your hand. Shaking them off for the birds costs you nothing. The Kural says base people will not give even that much to someone gentle who asks, but they will hand over anything to a bully who threatens them.
kurals.university: The image is precise: eerngai (ஈர்ங்கை, 'the wet hand') just washed after a meal, which the base will not even vidhir (விதிர், 'shake') so that a few grains fall to others. They give only to the kodiru udaikkum koonkaiyar (கொடிறுடைக்கும் கூன்கையர், 'those with bent, clenched hands that break the jaw'). Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesikan read koonkai as the fist curled to strike; Kalaignar makes the contrast explicit between the poor, who get nothing, and the thugs, who get what they demand. The couplet joins the chapter's themes of meanness and fear (cf. 1075). Pope: 'From off their moistened hands no clinging grain they shake, / Unless to those with clenched fist their jaws who break.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But charity performed with the expectation of some return, or with a desire for fruitive results, or in a grudging mood, is said to be charity in the mode of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita ranks grudging giving, or giving for some return, as a lower, rajasic kind of charity.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's base man gives only grudgingly, and only when forced, which the Gita would place well below true giving.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.21 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; reasonable on grudging giving, though the Gita does not mention giving under threat.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to give freely and cheerfully, not reluctantly or because they are compelled.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's base man gives only 'of necessity', the very opposite of Paul's cheerful giver.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); close on giving only under compulsion.

islam.quote_or_event: “they come not to prayer except while they are lazy and that they do not spend except while they are unwilling.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes hypocrites who give only reluctantly, against their will.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's base, they part with nothing willingly.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; strong on unwilling giving, though without the Kural's image of force.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A lower level than that is giving him with sadness.”
judaism.explanation: In Maimonides' ladder of charity, the lowest rung is giving to the poor grudgingly, with a sad face.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's base man does not reach even this lowest rung unless he is forced.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:14 (tr. Eliyahu Touger, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a reasonable fit on grudging giving, though Maimonides still counts it as charity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts the miser, who does not even value generosity, with the wise person who delights in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is this miser, who will not part with crumbs unless compelled.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; reasonable on miserliness, without the element of yielding to force.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those mean persons are of the nature of the chisel, which without being struck will not even penetrate a tender leaf, though resting upon it; they will give nothing to the kind-hearted, but will give anything to those who employ force, if they meet them.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar compares the mean to a chisel that cuts nothing unless it is hammered: they give nothing to gentle people but everything to those who use force.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's couplet in another image: the base give only to those who strike them.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 36.5, chapter 'Baseness or Envy' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text and a near one-to-one parallel, used because no canonical scripture comes as close.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, asks the suitors in his own hall for scraps, the arrogant Antinous refuses him anything and hurls a footstool at him, though the food he withholds is not even his own.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antinous gives nothing to the weak man who asks humbly, and is later destroyed by the very man he despised.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's base man, Antinous will not spare a crumb for someone who cannot force him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; good on refusing the humble, but it lacks the Kural's point that the base yield to force.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes meanness (aneleutheria) as a vice of deficiency in giving and excess in taking, and calls it incurable and more natural to people than prodigality, noting that some mean people refuse to give even from fear that they will be asked for more.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the mean man's refusal to give is a settled vice, the opposite of the liberal person who gives gladly to the right people.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's base man shows Aristotle's meanness in its sharpest form, giving nothing unless compelled.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: General paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; reasonable on meanness, without the element of yielding to force.

kurals.tamil:
சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர் கரும்புபோல்
கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sollap payanpaduvar saandror karumbupol
kollap payanpadum keezh.
kurals.meaning: The noble help you as soon as you tell them your need; the base, like sugarcane, give their juice only when they are crushed.
kurals.elementary: To get juice from sugarcane, you have to squeeze and crush it hard. A good person helps you as soon as you ask nicely. A mean person is like the sugarcane: he gives nothing until he is squeezed.
kurals.university: The couplet sets the saandror (சான்றோர், 'the noble, the perfect in virtue', the subject of ch. 99) against the keezh. The noble are solla (சொல்ல, 'on being told') useful: as Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss it, they give as soon as the needy describe their want. The base, karumbu pol (கரும்புபோல், 'like sugarcane'), yield only kolla (கொல்ல, 'on being crushed, killed'). Parimelazhagar takes kolla as being pressed to the point of torment, as cane is crushed in a mill; Pope's prose gloss follows ('only when they are tortured to death'). The image recurs in Tamil didactic poetry, though there the sweetness of crushed cane is sometimes used for the noble who stay sweet under pressure. Pope's verse: 'The good to those will profit yield fair words who use; / The base, like sugar-cane, will profit those who bruise.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That gift which is given out of duty, at the proper time and place, to a worthy person, and without expectation of return, is considered to be charity in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes the highest, sattvic giving: given freely, out of duty, with no thought of return.
hinduism.tie_back: This is how the Kural's saandror give, as soon as they are asked, in contrast to the base who must be crushed.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.20 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a reasonable fit for the noble half of the couplet only.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable, an unjust judge finally grants a widow's plea only because her constant pressure wears him down.
christianity.tie_back: The unjust judge is the Kural's sugarcane: he gives only when squeezed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); close on yielding only under pressure, though the parable's own point is about persistence in prayer.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Saying], "We feed you only for the face [i.e., approval] of Allāh. We wish not from you reward or gratitude."”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the righteous who feed the needy freely, seeking nothing in return.
islam.tie_back: These are the Kural's saandror, who give at a word, unlike the base who must be crushed like cane.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; fits only the noble half of the couplet.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who desires that he himself should give, and that others should give: he is a pious man; He who desires that he himself should not give and that others too should not give: he is a wicked man.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah sorts givers by their willingness, calling the willing giver pious and the one who wants no giving at all wicked.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it judges people by whether they give freely or have to be forced.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:13 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (excerpt); reasonable on willing versus unwilling givers, without the image of pressure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A person of integrity gives a gift with a sense of conviction. A person of integrity gives a gift attentively. A person of integrity gives a gift in season. A person of integrity gives a gift with an empathetic heart.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes how a good person gives: with conviction, care, good timing and sympathy.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's saandror give in this way, promptly and with empathy, as soon as they hear of a need.
buddhism.source: Sappurisadana Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 5.148 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; 'in season' and 'empathetic heart' fit the noble half well, but the sutta says nothing about the base.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The high-born, even when they have not anything, will approach those who are in want, and be a prop when they totter.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar says that the truly noble seek out the needy and support them even when they themselves have little.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's saandror, who give as soon as they learn of need, the opposite of the cane that yields only when crushed.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 15.10, chapter 'High Birth' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text that fits the noble half of the couplet only.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable of the walnut tree, a tree by the roadside bears a rich crop, and passers-by beat its branches with sticks and stones to get the nuts.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tree complains that it is beaten by the very people who enjoy its fruit.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fable shares the Kural's image of a giver from whom goods come only by beating, though Aesop's sympathy lies with the tree.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, 'The Walnut-Tree' (tr. George Fyler Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified this session; only a weak next-best match, since the fable is about ingratitude and shares only the image of yield under blows.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca teaches that a benefit should be given readily and without delay, since a gift that has to be dragged out of the giver, or that clings long to his hands, loses most of its value and earns little gratitude.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, promptness is part of what makes a gift a real benefit.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's ideal giver is the Kural's saandror; the gift wrung out under pressure is the base man's.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the opening of Book II, not verified verbatim this session; a strong fit on prompt versus extracted giving.

kurals.tamil:
உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின் பிறர்மேல்
வடுக்காண வற்றாகும் கீழ்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uduppadhoovum unbadhoovum kaanin pirarmel
vadukkaana vatraagum keezh.
kurals.meaning: When the base see others wearing good clothes and eating good food, they become experts at finding faults in them.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a classmate gets new shoes and a nice lunch. A jealous child might say, 'Those shoes are ugly' or 'Your lunch smells funny,' just because they feel envious. The Kural says base people do this: they invent faults in others because they cannot stand to see them happy.
kurals.university: The couplet describes envy (azhukkaaru, the subject of ch. 17) turned into fault-finding. Uduppadhum unbadhum (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம், with alapedai lengthening: 'what they wear and what they eat') are the most ordinary signs of others' well-being; on seeing them, the keezh become vatru (வற்று, 'strong, capable') at vadu kaana (வடுக்காண, 'finding a blemish'). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read envy as the cause and deliberate fault-finding as the result; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the base may even try to create a blemish (வடு உண்டாக்கவும் முயல்வான்). Pope: 'If neighbours clothed and fed he see, the base / Is mighty man some hidden fault to trace.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Duryodhana returns from the Pandavas' splendid assembly hall at Indraprastha burning with envy at their prosperity, tells his father he cannot bear to see their wealth, and plots the dice game to ruin them.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana's envy at the Pandavas' good fortune turns into scheming against them.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural's keezh: the sight of others' well-being drives him to find a way to harm them.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta sub-parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a central episode; strong on envy at others' prosperity, though Duryodhana schemes rather than merely finding fault.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.”
christianity.explanation: Envious officials, jealous of Daniel's high position, search his life for a fault to accuse him of.
christianity.tie_back: They are the Kural's base men, roused by another's success to hunt for blemishes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); close on envious fault-finding, provoked by status rather than food and clothing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Or do they envy people for what Allāh has given them of His bounty?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes those who resent the blessings God has given to others.
islam.tie_back: This is the envy at others' well-being that, in the Kural, drives the base to look for faults.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (excerpt); strong on envy of others' blessings, without the fault-finding.

judaism.quote_or_event: “envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ha-Kappar names envy as one of three passions that destroy a person.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural shows envy at work in the base, poisoning their view of anyone who prospers.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:21 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; reasonable on envy as a vice, but brief and without fault-finding.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes how readily people sift out others' faults while hiding their own.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is this eager winnower of others' faults, set in motion by envy.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; strong on fault-finding, though without the trigger of envy at others' comforts.

jainism.quote_or_event: “what are those wretches' tongues made of, who, standing in the presence of those persons, declare their faults, for the purpose of destroying their reputation?”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter 'Baseness or Envy', the Jain Naladiyar condemns those who announce others' faults in order to ruin their good name.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's keezh, skilled at finding blemishes in others out of envy.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 36.3, chapter 'Baseness or Envy' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (excerpt); a Tamil Jain text, strong on malicious fault-finding in a chapter explicitly about envy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid describes Envy (Invidia) as a figure who wastes away at the sight of others' success and is tormented by others' happiness; sent by Minerva, she poisons Aglauros with jealousy of her sister's good fortune.
greek_mythology.explanation: Envy in the myth cannot bear to see others thrive and turns that pain into malice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ovid's Envy is the Kural's base man made into a goddess: others' well-being is what torments her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage (a Roman telling of Greek myth); strong on envy at others' success.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines envy as hatred that makes a person sad at another's good fortune and glad at another's misfortune.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, envy is a form of hatred, and it naturally leads one to belittle the person envied.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shows the same passion in action: the base, pained by others' comforts, look for faults to bring them down.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Affects 23
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; a good fit on envy, though Spinoza defines it rather than describing fault-finding.

kurals.tamil:
எற்றிற் குரியர் கயவரொன்று உற்றக்கால்
விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Etrir kuriyar kayavarondru utrakkaal
vitrarku uriyar viraindhu.
kurals.meaning: What are the base good for? When trouble comes, they are quick to sell themselves; that is all they are fit for.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a team captain who, the moment the game gets hard, switches to the other team because they promise him a prize. He cannot be trusted. The Kural says base people are like that: at the first sign of trouble, they will sell out anyone, even themselves.
kurals.university: The chapter, and the whole Porutpal, ends with a rhetorical question: etrirku uriyar (எற்றிற்கு உரியர், 'for what are they fit?'). The answer: ondru utrakkaal (ஒன்று உற்றக்கால், 'when some calamity comes') they are fit vitrarku (விற்றற்கு, 'for selling', i.e. selling themselves) viraindhu (விரைந்து, 'quickly'). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read it as the base hastening to sell themselves to others to escape a misfortune; Puliyur Kesikan adds that they are fit for no other work; Solomon Pappaiah extends it to profit or loss, saying they make themselves others' slaves. The final sarcasm returns to the first couplet: the base have the human form but none of the steadfastness that gives a person worth. Pope: 'For what is base man fit, if griefs assail? / Himself to offer, there and then, for sale!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, to keep his promised word to the sage Vishvamitra, sold his wife, his son and finally himself into servitude, enduring every hardship rather than break faith.
hinduism.explanation: Harishchandra's self-sale is the noble opposite of the Kural's: he sells himself to keep his truth, not to escape trouble.
hinduism.tie_back: The contrast sharpens the Kural's point: the base sell themselves to save their skins, while the noble suffer anything to keep faith.
hinduism.source: Markandeya Purana, Harishchandra episode (tr. F. E. Pargiter)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known story used as a contrast; only a next-best match, since Harishchandra's self-sale is virtuous, not base.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.”
christianity.explanation: Judas goes to the chief priests and offers to betray Jesus for money.
christianity.tie_back: Judas is the Kural's base man, ready to sell himself and his loyalty for a price.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); strong on selling out, though Judas acts from greed rather than to escape a calamity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who exchange the covenant of Allāh and their [own] oaths for a small price will have no share in the Hereafter”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an condemns those who sell their solemn word for a little worldly gain.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's base, they are quick to sell what should never be for sale.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (excerpt); reasonable on selling oneself cheaply, without the element of calamity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esau said: ‘Behold, I am at the point to die; and what profit shall the birthright do to me?’ And Jacob said: ‘Swear to me first’; and he swore unto him; and he sold his birthright unto Jacob.”
judaism.explanation: Faint with hunger, Esau sells his birthright on the spot for a bowl of lentils.
judaism.tie_back: Esau is the Kural's base man exactly: at the first hardship he hastens to sell what is most precious.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; near one-to-one on selling oneself quickly under pressure of trouble.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The good renounce (attachment for) everything. The virtuous do not prattle with a yearning for pleasures. The wise show no elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the wise stay steady whether fortune or misfortune comes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the opposite: the first trouble knocks him off balance and he sells himself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a next-best contrast on steadiness in adversity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If any misfortune happens and he suffers pain, he should cheerfully steady his mind, and bear the ills that attack him.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on the twenty-two hardships (parishaha), Mahavira teaches the monk to meet misfortune with a steady mind and not be defeated by it.
jainism.tie_back: This is the opposite of the Kural's base man, who gives himself away the moment trouble comes.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable canonical contrast on steadfastness in misfortune.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Thermopylae, the Malian Ephialtes went to Xerxes hoping for a large reward and showed the Persians the mountain path around the pass, betraying the Greeks who held it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ephialtes sold out his own side for gain at the decisive moment, and his name became a byword for traitor.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ephialtes is the Kural's base man, ready to sell himself and others when the crisis comes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; Greek history rather than myth, and a reasonable fit on selling out in a crisis.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is you who know yourself, how much you are worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself; for men sell themselves at various prices.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus says each person decides how cheaply he will sell his integrity, and the Stoic refuses to sell it at all.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the one whose price is lowest: he sells himself at the first trouble.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; near one-to-one on selling oneself.
